Chapter 6: Weathering Storms—Leadership in the Age of Division
The years after Nancy’s historic rise to Speaker were anything but peaceful. The country’s mood had shifted, and it felt like the ground was always moving beneath everyone’s feet. One crisis would fade, and another would take its place. Trust in our institutions seemed to be slipping away, and the familiar rules of politics? They just didn’t hold like they used to.
In the middle of all this, Nancy’s daily life was a blur of urgent phone calls, tense meetings, and that ever-present feeling of uncertainty. Sometimes, even the most experienced lawmakers looked lost—unsure of how to bridge the growing divides between parties, regions, and even generations. The Capitol itself had changed. It felt less like a place for debate, and more like a battlefield.
One winter stands out, when a government shutdown dragged on for weeks. The mood in Washington grew heavy. Staffers shuffled through the halls, their eyes tired from long days and longer nights. The usual buzz was replaced by a kind of waiting—waiting for someone to make the first move, for a deal to come together, for the country to start moving forward again.
In those moments, Nancy’s approach became both simple and hard-earned: keep talking, keep listening, and above all—never let frustration turn into despair.
She’d gather her team into a cramped office, everyone clutching their coffee. She’d remind them that every crisis was more than a challenge—it was a test of character. “We don’t get to choose the times we live in,” she’d say, “but we do get to choose how we respond.” For some, those words felt like a lifeline—a reminder that, even in the darkest hours, there was important work to do, and people counting on them to do it.
Most of us never see the toll public service can take—the birthdays missed, the sleepless nights, the constant awareness that every single decision will leave someone disappointed. But Nancy understood something: leadership isn’t about being popular. It’s about being steady. When tempers flared or negotiations hit a wall, she’d fall back on what she’d learned as a child—patience, preparation, and that quiet belief that progress is always possible, even if it comes an inch at a time.
As the years rolled on, the challenges didn’t get any smaller. New voices entered the political arena—some eager to shake things up, others determined to defend the old ways. Through it all, Nancy played many roles: part conductor, part counselor. She guided her colleagues through the noise, helped them find common ground, and kept reminding them that the work was bigger than any one person or moment.
Here’s the heart of it: in times of deep division, the most important thing a leader can offer isn’t certainty—it’s hope. The belief that together, we really can weather any storm.
